messages.author: 0b0e14897bf1bea4
messages.subject: do the loop portion in translated C++ code in parallel
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have an idea to fast the computing of the stan model. Usually in a complex model with random effect, we need to sample the random effect for each subject, and calculate the likelihood. It would be very time consuming if the data  involves a large number of subjects, but this part can be done independently for each subject. I am thinking doing these parts via GPU parallel computing with thousands of core
thousands of cores
. First, translating the Stan model to C++ code. Then find the loop in the C++ code doing these part of sampling and calculation. Modified that part of code to achieve the same goal in parallel on GPU. Compile the modified code and run the model.
Please let me know whether it is feasible and some guidance to start. I appreciate.

Kan

On Thursday, July 21, 2016 at 3:05:41 PM UTC-4, Kan Li wrote:

It would be very time consuming if the data  involves a large number of subjects, but this part can be done independently for each subject. I am thinking doing these parts via GPU parallel computing with thousands of core
thousands of cores

That is currently only realistic in specific cases. If the likelihood does not utilize autodiff (i.e. all the var inputs are stripped down to doubles, the score is calculated analytically, and the derivative information is reattached to the output), it could be done but the likelihood evaluation for each observation would need to take a long time to overcome the repeated offloading to the GPU and the summation on the CPU of all the pieces returned by the GPU. We don't have any way to determine that automatically, so it would have to be something done by a human.  Also, GPU operations are more advanced for floats than doubles, but Stan does not do floats.

Ben

parts: Not clear from your question if this is obvious or not but with Stan there's the additional complication of autodiff being the more expensive operation than the straight likelihood computation so optimizing anything else is likely to be a dead end unless you've benchmarked it to demonstrate that you know what you're optimizing and why. Krzysztof

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: do the loop portion in translated C++ code in parallel
parts:
On Thursday, July 21, 2016 at 11:57:50 PM UTC-4, Kan Li wrote:
Do you think using multiple cores to do the task of "normal_log<propto__>(get_base1(vary_herd_index,j,"vary_herd_index",1), 0, sigma_herd_index)" simultaneously and return the results would save sometime?
No. But you would be comparing it to an overly slow version anyway. This line
for ( j in 1:N_herd_index ) vary_herd_index[j] ~ normal( 0 , sigma_herd_index );

should just be

vary_herd_index ~ normal( 0 , sigma_herd_index );

which evaluates very quickly on a CPU. None of the basic univariate density functions with accumulating analytical derivatives are going to evaluate slowly enough to justify the trip to a GPU and then summing the results on a GPU. It might be worthwhile if you are doing a multivariate normal density with 10000 dimensions or integrating an ODE for each person or something.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: do the loop portion in translated C++ code in parallel
parts:
We get this suggestion a lot.

Autodiff has side effects, so parallelization is
non-trivial.

In theory, larger chunks of autodiff can be done in
parallel and checkpointed. Then they have to all
be put back together into derivatives of the whole
system.

Parallelization has portability issues, though we're
about to move to C++11 that will make this easier.

If you need to do this now and your models are simple,
you might want to look at TensorFlow.

- Bob
